tldr: A **coordinator** agent splits a big task into distinct parts and hands each to a **subagent** through the spawn tool — **`Task`** on the exam, **`Agent`** in the current docs. A subagent starts with a **fresh context**: the *only* thing it receives is the prompt the coordinator writes, and only its **final message** comes back. So a well-built coordinator (1) is allowed to spawn, (2) decomposes broadly enough, (3) puts the complete findings and their sources in every prompt, (4) emits independent calls together in one response, (5) keeps every result flowing through itself, and (6) reviews the draft for gaps and re-delegates.
mentalModel: The coordinator is a project manager who can only send **emails** to contractors: a contractor sees just the email — never the manager's inbox — and sends back only a final report. Leave the facts out of the email and the work is wrong; brief only one contractor and the project has a hole.
whatItIs:
The docs describe subagents as separate agent instances your main agent spawns for focused subtasks, with four benefits:
**context isolation**, **parallelisation**, **specialised instructions** and **tool restrictions**. The exam guide turns that
into an architecture: a **hub-and-spoke** system where a coordinator decomposes the work, delegates, aggregates, and manages
*all* communication and error handling (Guide §6 · TS 1.2, pp.5–6), plus the mechanics of spawning and passing context
(TS 1.3, pp.6–7).

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember and where the exam names it**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hub-and-spoke coordinator | A switchboard: every call goes through the operator, so the operator knows what is happening and can react to a failure. | ⭐ TS 1.2 · Knowledge 1, Skill 4 · pp.5–6 |
| 2 | Isolated context | Each subagent is a new hire on day one: it knows only what the briefing says. | ⭐ TS 1.2 · Knowledge 2 · pp.5–6; TS 1.3 · Knowledge 2 · pp.6–7 |
| 3 | Decomposition & selection | A manager splits the job by workstream, skips workstreams this job doesn't need — and a plan that covers one workstream has a hole. | ⭐ TS 1.2 · Knowledge 3–4, Skills 1–2 · pp.5–6 |
| 4 | The spawn tool | The coordinator's badge: without `Task` on the allowed list, the door doesn't open. | ⭐ TS 1.3 · Knowledge 1 · pp.6–7 |
| 5 | AgentDefinition | A job description: the role, its instructions, its toolbox. | ⭐ TS 1.3 · Knowledge 3 · pp.6–7 |
| 6 | Explicit context & structured findings | Hand over a labelled file (claim · source · page), not a summary in your own words. | ⭐ TS 1.3 · Skills 1–2 · pp.6–7 |
| 7 | Parallel spawning | Send all the briefing emails at once, not one after another. | ⭐ TS 1.3 · Skill 3 · pp.6–7 |
| 8 | Iterative refinement | Proofread the draft, then send the missing chapter back to be written. | ⭐ TS 1.2 · Skill 3 · pp.5–6 |
| 9 | Goals, not procedures | Give the contractor the goal and the quality bar — a rigid checklist breaks the moment the situation differs. | ⭐ TS 1.3 · Skill 4 · pp.6–7 |
| 10 | Session fork | Photocopy the case file: two investigators, one shared starting point, the original untouched. | ⭐ TS 1.3 · Knowledge 4 · pp.6–7 |

**What a subagent receives — and doesn't** (docs, non-fork subagent)

| # | Receives | Does NOT receive |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Its own system prompt (`AgentDefinition.prompt`) and the spawn tool's **prompt string** | The parent's conversation history or tool results |
| 2 | Project CLAUDE.md files (unless the definition sets `omitClaudeMd`) | Preloaded skill content, unless listed in `skills` |
| 3 | Its tool definitions (all available to subagents, or only the ones in `tools`) | The parent's system prompt |

**AgentDefinition fields** (docs — the exam names *description*, *system prompt* and *tool restrictions*)

| # | Field | Required? | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `description` | yes | When Claude should use this subagent — how it chooses |
| 2 | `prompt` | yes | The subagent's system prompt: its role and behaviour |
| 3 | `tools` | no | Allowed tool names; **omitted = inherits every tool available to subagents**; a tool left out isn't in its session at all |
| 4 | `disallowedTools` · `model` · `skills` · `memory` · `mcpServers` · `maxTurns` · `background` … | no | Further optional controls (beyond what the exam names) — see **Tools & permissions** below |

---

### 🧰 Tools & permissions — who gets what (coordinator → subagent)

> 🧭 **Mental model:** the coordinator's toolbox is the **shop floor**; `tools` is the **list a subagent is handed**, and
> `disallowedTools` is **what's taken out of the box first**. `allowedTools` is not a toolbox at all — it's the list of tools
> that **don't need a signature** before use. Mixing up "can it see the tool?" with "is it pre-approved?" is the trap.

**Grid 1 — each setting, where it lives, and what happens if you leave it blank** (docs, 2026-09-28)

| # | Setting | Set on | Controls | If left blank / omitted | Reaches the subagent? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `allowedTools` / `allowed_tools` | the **query** (coordinator) | **Permission** — listed tools run **without asking**. It does **not** add or remove tools | Nothing is pre-approved; calls that need approval go to the permission mode / `canUseTool` | ✅ Permission rules are inherited from the parent conversation |
| 2 | `disallowedTools` / `disallowed_tools` | the **query** (coordinator) | Bare name (`"Bash"`) **removes the tool** from the request; scoped rule (`"Bash(rm *)"`) **denies matching calls** in every mode | Nothing removed or denied | ✅ Deny rules apply inside subagents too; a removed tool isn't in the main conversation, so there's nothing to inherit |
| 3 | `tools` | the **AgentDefinition** (one subagent) | **Availability** — the subagent gets **only** these tools | ⭐ **Inherits every tool available to subagents** (grid 2) | — (it *is* the subagent's list) |
| 4 | `disallowedTools` | the **AgentDefinition** | Removes tools from **this** subagent (`mcp__server`, `mcp__*` patterns allowed) | Nothing removed | — |
| 5 | `permissionMode` | the **AgentDefinition** | The subagent's permission mode | Runs in the parent's mode | ⚠️ If the parent is in `bypassPermissions`, `acceptEdits` or auto, the subagent uses the **parent's** mode and ignores this field; `bypassPermissions` here is never applied |
| 6 | `mcpServers` | the **AgentDefinition** | MCP servers for this agent (by name or inline config) | The main conversation's **MCP tools are still inherited** | ✅ All MCP tools are kept (foreground and background) |
| 7 | `skills` | the **AgentDefinition** | Skill content **preloaded** at startup | Nothing preloaded — the subagent can still invoke skills with the Skill tool | ❌ Preloaded skill content is not inherited |
| 8 | `model` | the **AgentDefinition** | Model for this subagent (`'inherit'` = the main model) | Claude Code picks by its subagent model order | Only with `'inherit'` |
| 9 | The spawn tool (`Task` in the guide, `Agent` in the docs) | the coordinator's tools / `allowedTools` | Whether the coordinator can spawn | ⭐ **Exam:** `allowedTools` must include `"Task"`. 📘 Docs: `Agent` is a tool that doesn't ask before running in default mode | Nested spawning allowed down to 3 levels; at the limit `Agent` is withheld |

**Grid 2 — what a (non-fork) subagent inherits from the coordinator**

| # | Item | Inherited? | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Built-in tools of the main conversation | ✅ when `tools` is omitted | Minus the always-removed ones (row 9) |
| 2 | MCP tools of the main conversation | ✅ | Kept for foreground **and** background subagents |
| 3 | Permission rules (allow / deny) | ✅ | Deny rules such as `Bash(git push *)` apply in subagents too |
| 4 | Permission mode | ⚠️ depends | Grid 1, row 5 |
| 5 | Hooks from settings files, managed policy, plugins | ✅ | A settings `PreToolUse` hook runs before every subagent tool call |
| 6 | CLAUDE.md files | ✅ | Unless the definition sets `omitClaudeMd` |
| 7 | Extended thinking configuration | ✅ | — |
| 8 | ⭐ Coordinator's conversation history and tool results | ❌ | Pass what it needs **in the spawn prompt** (TS 1.3) |
| 9 | Tools always removed from subagents | ❌ | `AskUserQuestion`, `EnterPlanMode`, `ExitPlanMode` (unless plan mode), `EndConversation`, `ScheduleWakeup`, `WaitForMcpServers`, `Workflow`, and `Agent` at the depth limit |
| 10 | Background subagents | ⚠️ fewer built-ins | Only `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `LSP`, `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Edit`, `Write`, `NotebookEdit`, `WebFetch`, `WebSearch`, `TodoWrite`, `Skill`, `ToolSearch`, `EnterWorktree`, `ExitWorktree`, `Monitor`, `TaskStop`, `SendMessage`, `Artifact` (+ all MCP tools) |
| 11 | The parent's system prompt | ❌ | It gets its own `prompt` |

**Grid 3 — worked examples: what the subagent ends up with**

| # | Coordinator (query) | AgentDefinition | Subagent's tools | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | — | `tools` omitted, `disallowedTools` omitted | Every tool available to subagents | Omitted = inherit (grid 2) |
| 2 | — | `tools=["Read","Grep","Glob"]` | `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob` | Listed = only those; others aren't in its session at all (no error, no prompt) |
| 3 | — | `disallowedTools=["Write","Edit"]` | Everything except `Write`, `Edit` | Removed from the inherited set |
| 4 | — | `tools=["Read","Edit"]`, `disallowedTools=["Edit"]` | `Read` | `disallowedTools` applied **first**; a tool in both is removed |
| 5 | `disallowed_tools=["Bash"]` | `tools` omitted | Everything except `Bash` | Bash was removed from the main conversation, so it can't be inherited |
| 6 | `allowed_tools=["Read"]` | `tools=["Bash"]` | `Bash` (asks for approval) | `allowedTools` is permission, not availability |
| 7 | — | `disallowedTools=["mcp__*"]` | Built-ins only | `mcp__*` removes every MCP tool |
| 8 | — | `tools=["Agent"]` at the depth limit | nothing → usually refused to launch | `Agent` is withheld at the limit; a `tools` list that resolves to nothing is usually refused |

**`Task` or `Agent`?** The guide says the spawn tool is **`Task`** and that `allowedTools` must include it. The current docs say
the tool is **`Agent`** — it shows up as `"Agent"` in `tool_use` blocks and as `"Task"` in the init tool list, `"Task"` was the
name before Claude Code v2.1.63, and the docs advise matching both. For the exam: **Task**. In real code today: know both.

**Hub-and-spoke vs nesting.** The guide's model has the coordinator route everything. The docs *also* let subagents spawn their
own subagents (default: 3 layers deep) and cap that with depth, concurrency (default 20 at once) and spend limits. Designing
for observability and error handling means keeping the coordinator in the middle, as the exam expects.
howItWorks:
1. **Allow spawning.** The coordinator's tool list includes the spawn tool (`Task`), and each subagent type has a definition:
   description, system prompt, tool restrictions.
2. **Decompose and select.** The coordinator reads the question, splits a broad one into *distinct* areas, and picks only the
   subagents this query needs — a simple question may need just one.
3. **Spawn — in one response.** Independent subagents are requested together, as several `Task` calls in a single coordinator
   response. All their `tool_result` blocks go back in one user message (the same rule you met in D1.1).
4. **Give complete context in the prompt.** Each subagent sees only its prompt. Put the goal, the quality criteria, and any earlier
   findings — as structured data with source URL, document and page — directly in it.
5. **Only the final message returns.** The subagent's own tool calls stay inside it; the coordinator receives its final message
   as the tool result.
6. **Aggregate, review, refine.** The coordinator combines results, checks coverage against the quality criteria, re-delegates
   targeted searches for gaps, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient — then answers.
7. **Fork, don't overwrite, to explore.** To try a different approach from a shared analysis baseline, fork the session: the fork
   is a new session with a copy of the history; the original is unchanged.

labIntro:
Pick a starting point and a scenario, **edit the code if you like, and press Run.** You write the *coordinator* — its prompt, the tool
list, and how each subagent is run and what comes back — against a **simulated** research model and a fake search backend. The variants
are the correct design plus eight ways to get it wrong: seven from the exam guide (⭐, exact bullets in the table below) and one from the
docs' own warnings. Some only break on the right scenario — that's what makes them distractors.

labScenarios.description: A broad question about AI and the creative industries. A good coordinator splits it into distinct areas (visual arts, music, film), delegates them, verifies, and synthesises a cited report.

labScenarios.title: Simple question — one lookup is enough
labScenarios.description: A one-fact question. A good coordinator picks ONE subagent; a fixed pipeline runs everything anyway.

variants.code:
from utils.mock_claude import MockClaude   # SIMULATED stand-in. In the real SDK the Task/Agent tool spawns subagents for you
from utils.research_backend import QUERY, TASK_TOOL, WEB_SEARCH_TOOL, run_research_tool

client = MockClaude()
MODEL = "mock-claude"

# Goal + quality criteria (not a step-by-step recipe). It also says: delegate in parallel, give each
# subagent complete context, and review the draft for gaps.
COORDINATOR_PROMPT = """ROLE: coordinator.
Goal: a cited report that covers ALL major areas of the topic; every claim needs a source.
Quality bar: no major area missing, no duplicated research - give each subagent a distinct area.
Choose only the subagents the question actually needs.
Delegate independent areas in parallel (all Task calls in ONE response).
Subagents cannot see this conversation: put the complete context they need in each prompt.
When a draft comes back, review it for gaps and re-delegate targeted searches for anything missing."""

AGENTS = {   # AgentDefinition-style: a description, a system prompt, and TOOL RESTRICTIONS per subagent type
    "searcher":    {"description": "Finds sources for ONE area", "tools": [WEB_SEARCH_TOOL],
                    "prompt": "ROLE: searcher. Search for the area you are given; return findings as JSON with source metadata."},
    "analyst":     {"description": "Verifies findings", "tools": [],
                    "prompt": "ROLE: analyst. Verify the findings you are given; keep every source."},
    "synthesizer": {"description": "Writes the cited report", "tools": [],
                    "prompt": "ROLE: synthesizer. Write a cited report ONLY from the findings you are given."},
}
ALLOWED_TOOLS = [TASK_TOOL]   # the coordinator's allowedTools must include the spawn tool ("Task" on the exam; "Agent" in current docs)


def run_subagent(subagent_type, prompt):
    agent = AGENTS[subagent_type]
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]       # the prompt string is the ONLY thing a subagent receives
    for _ in range(6):
        r = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=512, system=agent["prompt"],
                                   tools=agent["tools"], messages=messages)
        if r.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return "".join(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text")   # only the FINAL message goes back
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})
        results = [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": run_research_tool(b.name, b.input)}
                   for b in r.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    raise RuntimeError("subagent did not finish")


messages = [{"role": "user", "content": QUERY}]
for turn in range(1, 11):
    r = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024, system=COORDINATOR_PROMPT,
                               tools=ALLOWED_TOOLS, messages=messages)
    calls = [b for b in r.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    print(f"coordinator turn {turn}: stop_reason = {r.stop_reason}, Task calls in this response: {len(calls)}")
    if r.stop_reason == "tool_use":
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})
        results = []
        for b in calls:                                     # every Task call in the response gets a result...
            out = run_subagent(b.input["subagent_type"], b.input["prompt"])
            print(f"   {b.input['subagent_type']:11s} -> {out[:70]!r}")
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": out})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})   # ...all in ONE user message
        continue
    if r.stop_reason == "end_turn":
        print("FINAL REPORT:\n" + "".join(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text"))
        break
    raise RuntimeError(f"unhandled stop_reason: {r.stop_reason}")
else:
    raise RuntimeError("coordinator did not finish within 10 turns")

distractors.name: A · No spawn tool in allowedTools
distractors.looks: The subagents are defined and described, so delegation should just happen.
distractors.fails: Nothing is callable: the coordinator answers alone, unsourced — and nothing errors.
distractors.instead: Put the spawn tool (`Task` on the exam, `Agent` in current docs) in the coordinator's allowed tools.

distractors.name: B · Assume subagents inherit context
distractors.looks: The coordinator obviously has the findings, so “write the report from what we have” should work.
distractors.fails: A subagent starts fresh: only its prompt reaches it, and nothing is shared between invocations — it has no findings.
distractors.instead: Put the complete findings, with source metadata, in the subagent's prompt.

distractors.name: C · Always run the full pipeline
distractors.looks: A fixed search → verify → write sequence is predictable and easy to reason about.
distractors.fails: One-fact questions pay for three subagents; broad ones never get decomposed.
distractors.instead: Let the coordinator select subagents by query complexity.

distractors.name: D · Decompose too narrowly
distractors.looks: Every subagent succeeds and the report reads fluently — it must be complete.
distractors.fails: The coordinator only assigned one area, so the report silently covers a third of the topic.
distractors.instead: Partition the topic into all its major areas; make coverage a stated quality criterion.

distractors.name: E · One Task call per turn
distractors.looks: Waiting for each result is simple, and the final report is identical.
distractors.fails: Independent work is serialised: more coordinator turns and more wall-clock time.
distractors.instead: Emit all independent Task calls in a single response.

distractors.name: F · Route results around the coordinator
distractors.looks: Handing findings straight to the next subagent saves a hop.
distractors.fails: The coordinator is blind: it can't see failures, handle errors consistently or answer from what it never received.
distractors.instead: All subagent communication goes through the coordinator.

distractors.name: G · No gap review or re-delegation
distractors.looks: The first draft came back, so the coordinator can just return it.
distractors.fails: A failed or missing area is never noticed; the report is silently incomplete.
distractors.instead: Evaluate the draft for gaps, re-delegate targeted searches, re-invoke synthesis.

distractors.name: H · Return the whole subagent transcript
distractors.looks: More information can't hurt — the coordinator can see everything the subagent did.
distractors.fails: The coordinator's context balloons with intermediate calls, defeating context isolation.
distractors.instead: Return only the subagent's final message, as a concise structured summary with sources.

questions.q: To save a round trip, a developer lets the synthesis subagent call the web-search subagent directly whenever it spots a gap. Within a week, 6% of reports contain unexplained holes. In each case a direct search timed out, and the coordinator's logs have no record of the exchange, so nothing retried it. What is the most effective change?
opts: Add retries with exponential backoff to the synthesis subagent's direct calls to the web-search subagent.
Route every exchange between subagents through the coordinator, so it sees, handles and logs each result.
Have the synthesis subagent write each direct call to a shared log file that the coordinator reads afterwards.
Merge synthesis and web search into one subagent, so that no handoff between them can fail without being seen.
questions.explain: In the hub-and-spoke pattern the coordinator manages all communication, so it can observe each exchange, handle errors and decide on recovery. A makes a timeout less likely but still leaves failures hidden from the coordinator. C gives visibility after the fact, with no chance to act on it. D gives up specialisation and context isolation to solve a routing problem.

questions.q: Asked to research “renewable energy adoption in Europe”, the system returns a well-cited report that covers only solar power in Germany and Spain. Every subagent finished without errors, and synthesis used all the findings it received. The coordinator's log lists its assignments: “German solar subsidies”, “Spanish solar capacity” and “EU solar panel imports”. What should you change first?
opts: Add a coverage check to the synthesis subagent so it flags energy sources that are missing from its findings.
Broaden the web-search subagent's queries so that each search also returns wind, hydro and other countries.
Make the coordinator's decomposition cover the request's full scope before it assigns any subtasks at all.
Add two more search subagents so that the system collects a larger volume of sources for every run it does.
questions.explain: The log shows the gap was created at decomposition: no subagent was ever asked about wind, hydro or most countries. Every downstream agent did what it was assigned. A would notice the gap after the work was done instead of preventing it. B makes subagents stray outside their assignments. D adds more volume inside the same narrow scope.

questions.q: Users ask everything from “What year was the EU ETS launched?” to “Compare carbon-pricing schemes across five regions”. Every query runs all four subagents in sequence. Logs show simple factual questions take a median of 3.5 minutes and cost the same as complex comparisons. Which design change best fixes this?
opts: Have the coordinator assess each query's needs and invoke only the subagents that query actually requires.
Put a keyword-based router in front of the coordinator that sends short queries to a single-agent pipeline.
Run the four subagents in parallel instead of in sequence, so every query takes less wall-clock time overall.
Cache the four subagents' outputs by query text, so that repeated factual questions can skip the pipeline.
questions.explain: The coordinator should choose which subagents to invoke based on what each query needs, instead of always running the full pipeline. B is an over-engineered routing layer that duplicates the coordinator's job, using keywords. C cuts latency but still pays for four agents on a one-line fact. D helps only exact repeats.

questions.q: Two search subagents receive the same brief: “find recent evidence on battery recycling”. Their results overlap by about 70%, and the synthesis subagent spends roughly a third of its context de-duplicating them. Coverage of recycling policy, one of the areas the user requested, is thin. What is the most effective change?
opts: Add a de-duplication step between search and synthesis that removes findings with near-identical content.
Tell both search subagents in their prompts to avoid returning results that the other subagent might find.
Replace both search subagents with one that runs twice as many queries, so overlap between them is impossible.
Give each search subagent a distinct slice of the scope, such as separate subtopics or different source types.
questions.explain: Partitioning the research scope between subagents removes duplicate work and makes each part of the request someone's job. A treats the symptom and leaves the policy gap. B asks each subagent to avoid results it cannot see, because subagents share no context. C removes the overlap by also removing the parallelism.

questions.q: A user asked for a report on “the EV market: regulation, market size and supply chains”. The first synthesis covers regulation and market size in depth but gives supply chains two sentences. The search logs show only 1 of 14 findings concerned supply chains. The coordinator currently returns the first synthesis to the user. What should the coordinator do?
opts: Return the report with a note telling the user that supply-chain coverage was limited by available sources.
Check the draft against the request, send targeted supply-chain queries to search, then rerun synthesis.
Ask the synthesis subagent to expand the supply-chain section using its general knowledge of the industry.
Rerun the whole pipeline from scratch with the same assignments, in the hope that a new run finds more sources.
questions.explain: An iterative refinement loop has the coordinator evaluate the output for gaps, re-delegate targeted queries, and synthesise again until coverage is enough. A ships a known gap. C fills the gap with unsourced content. D repeats the same assignments, so it will probably find the same one supply-chain source.

questions.q: A coordinator built with the Agent SDK has three well-described subagent definitions, and they load without errors. In 50 test runs it never delegates: it answers every research question itself, and the transcripts contain no spawn-tool calls. Its allowedTools list is ["WebSearch", "Read"]. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The subagent descriptions are too short for the coordinator to recognise when it should delegate work to them.
allowedTools lacks the subagent-spawning tool (“Task” in the guide; current docs call it “Agent”).
The coordinator's model is too small to plan multi-agent work, so it should be upgraded to a larger model tier.
The coordinator's system prompt must name each subagent before the SDK can make that subagent available.
questions.explain: A coordinator can invoke subagents only if its allowedTools includes the spawning tool. The allowedTools list in the stem is the clue. A could reduce delegation, but not to zero calls in 50 runs. C blames the model for a configuration gap. D describes a requirement that doesn't exist: definitions are passed as SDK configuration.

questions.q: The coordinator sends document-analysis work to the web-search subagent in about 25% of runs, and that subagent then tries to “analyse” PDFs with web search, which it cannot open. Both subagent definitions currently contain only a name and the coordinator's own system prompt. What should each subagent definition include?
opts: A longer name that states its role, plus a priority number the coordinator can use to break ties between agents.
Access to every tool in the system, so that whichever subagent is chosen can finish any task it is handed.
A clear description of when to use it, its own role-specific system prompt, and tools restricted to its role.
A few-shot block in the coordinator's prompt showing which requests go to which subagent, and no other change.
questions.explain: An agent definition carries a description (which the coordinator uses to choose), a system prompt for the role, and a tool restriction that keeps it in its lane. A invents a priority field. B over-provisions every agent and removes specialisation. D may improve routing a little, but it leaves each subagent generic and unrestricted.

questions.q: To research three independent regions, the coordinator spawns one search subagent, waits for its result, then spawns the next. Each search takes about 50 seconds, so the research phase takes 2.5 minutes. The three searches do not depend on each other. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Give one search subagent all three regions in a single prompt, so the coordinator needs only one spawn call.
Reduce each subagent's max_turns so every individual search finishes faster before the next one starts.
Spawn the three subagents across three consecutive coordinator turns, each with a shorter, simpler brief.
Have the coordinator emit all three spawn-tool calls in a single response, so the subagents run in parallel.
questions.explain: Several spawn-tool calls in one coordinator response run the subagents in parallel, so the phase takes about as long as the slowest search. A serialises the work inside one agent. B trades quality for speed and leaves the work serial. C is the separate-turns pattern that causes the delay.

questions.q: The coordinator prompts each search subagent with a numbered procedure: search site A, then site B, then summarise the top five results. Since site A added a paywall, 60% of subagent runs return thin findings built from site B alone, and none of them try other sources. What is the most effective change to the coordinator's prompts?
opts: State the research goal and the quality bar the findings must meet, and let each subagent decide how to get there.
Add a step 2b telling every subagent to search site C whenever site A returns a paywall or an empty results page.
Replace site A with site C in the procedure, and keep exactly the same numbered steps for every subagent that runs.
Give the subagents a larger max_turns budget, so they have time to complete every step of the procedure.
questions.explain: Coordinator prompts should specify goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedures, so subagents can adapt when a path fails. B and C patch this one failure and break again at the next change. D gives more time to follow a procedure that is itself the problem.

questions.q: Your monitoring counts subagent spawns by matching tool_use blocks named “Task”. After an Agent SDK upgrade, the dashboard has shown zero spawns for three days, yet the reports clearly still come from several subagents, and cost per report is unchanged. What is the most robust fix?
opts: Pin the Agent SDK to the previous version, so that the spawn tool keeps its old name in every transcript.
Count spawns by searching the coordinator's text for phrases like “delegating to” or “spawning a subagent”.
Match tool_use blocks named “Agent” or “Task”: current docs name the spawn tool Agent, with Task an alias.
Stop counting spawns and infer the number of subagents from the total token usage recorded for each run.
questions.explain: Current docs name the spawn tool Agent and keep Task as a legacy alias (the exam guide uses Task), so match both. A freezes you on an old SDK. B parses prose, which is unreliable. D guesses from a proxy.

questions.q: A main agent sends a subagent to map a legacy billing module. The subagent reads 40 files, runs a dozen searches, and then replies “Mapping complete.” Afterwards, the main agent cannot answer follow-up questions about any specific file, and the developer asks why the findings were “lost”. What explains it, and what is the fix?
opts: Only the subagent's final message returns to the parent, so ask it to return a structured summary of findings.
The subagent's context was cleared when it finished, so it must be resumed to recover the files it read.
The main agent's context window was too small to hold 40 files, so a larger model should coordinate instead.
Subagents share memory with the parent only in the foreground, so this subagent must not run in the background.
questions.explain: By design, only a subagent's final message returns to the parent. Its exploration stays in its own context, which is the point of isolation. So the subagent must be asked to return what matters, in a structured form. B misreads the problem: the parent never received the findings in the first place. C blames the window. D invents a memory-sharing rule.

faq.q: Is it called Task or Agent?
faq.a: The exam guide says **Task** and says `allowedTools` must include it. The current docs call the tool **Agent** (renamed in Claude Code v2.1.63; `Task` remains as a legacy alias) and use `"Agent"` in their `allowed_tools` examples. Answer with Task on the exam; in real code match both.

The docs say yes — by default up to 3 layers deep, adjustable, with concurrency (default 20) and spend limits. The exam's hub-and-spoke model keeps the coordinator in the middle for observability and error handling, so design that way.

faq.q: What actually comes back from a subagent?
faq.a: Its final message, as the spawn tool's result. Its own tool calls and results stay inside it. The parent may summarise the message in its own reply.

A subagent starts fresh (it gets only the prompt). A **fork** subagent inherits the parent conversation instead. Separately, a **session fork** copies a session's history into a new session so you can try another direction — the original is unchanged, but files are not branched.

faq.q: What happens past the concurrent-subagent limit?
faq.a: Per the docs, the spawn is refused with the text “Concurrent subagent limit reached” until the running count drops — it isn't queued. The playground's “Parallel spawning” tab lets you set the limit and watch the coordinator recover.

faq.q: Does the simulated coordinator behave like real Claude?
faq.a: No. It follows its system prompt by keyword (“parallel”, “gaps”, “step 1”…) so failures are reproducible. Real models interpret prompts far less literally — the mechanics (context isolation, the spawn tool, only the final message returning) are the documented part.
